lesson.title: The Real Number System: Rational and Irrational United
lesson.summary: Real numbers fill every point on the number line by combining the rational numbers with the irrational numbers, whose decimals never terminate or repeat.
lesson.body:
The real numbers are the union of the rational numbers and the irrational numbers, and together they fill in every single point on the number line without any gaps. Irrational numbers are numbers whose decimal expansions never terminate and never settle into a repeating pattern, which means they cannot be written as a fraction of two integers. The square root of 2 is a classic example: it equals approximately 1.41421356..., and this decimal continues forever with no repeating block. Pi, approximately 3.14159265..., is another famous irrational number that shows up whenever circles are involved.

You can picture the number system as a series of nested categories. Natural numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) sit inside the integers, which sit inside the rational numbers, which sit inside the real numbers. Irrational numbers are real numbers that sit entirely outside the rational numbers; they do not overlap with rationals at all. So the real numbers are made of exactly two non overlapping pieces: everything rational, and everything irrational. Every number you have worked with so far, and every number you will encounter in this course, is a real number.

Why does this distinction matter? Because some very ordinary operations produce irrational results even when you start with nice numbers. The square root of 2 arises naturally as the length of the diagonal of a unit square, by the Pythagorean relationship 1 squared plus 1 squared equals the diagonal squared, so the diagonal equals the square root of 2. No fraction of integers, no matter how carefully chosen, equals the square root of 2 exactly; this was proven by contradiction in ancient Greek mathematics and remains one of the earliest known proofs that an irrational number exists.

Worked example: classify the numbers -7, 0.6, the square root of 9, and the square root of 5. The number -7 is an integer, and every integer is rational, so it is a real number. The number 0.6 equals 3/5, a ratio of integers, so it is rational and real. The square root of 9 equals 3 exactly, because 3 times 3 is 9, so it is a whole number, an integer, and rational, hence real. The square root of 5 is not a perfect square; its decimal expansion, approximately 2.2360679..., never terminates or repeats, so it is irrational, yet still a real number.

Real numbers build on rational numbers by adding in everything rational numbers leave out, filling every remaining gap on the number line. This complete set is what makes the number line, covered next, a faithful and unbroken picture of quantity: every point on that line corresponds to exactly one real number, rational or irrational, and every real number corresponds to exactly one point. From here on, when a problem says find all real solutions, it means solutions can be rational or irrational, as long as they are somewhere on that line.
